forces: Piano and jazz band; orchestration by Ferde Grofé
performers: George Gershwin, piano; Paul Whiteman Concert Orchestra; Paul Whiteman, conductor
intro: Gershwin played the piano in the first recording of his Rhapsody in Blue, made in 1924 with Paul Whiteman’s band and with Ross Gorman’s sliding clarinet. Both sides of the record are heard here; this nine-minute version cuts about a third of the score.

sections.label: B · Train rhythms and stride piano
C · Broad tune and closing reprises
sections.mNote: The long melody is followed by the closing reprises.

cues.title: Clarinet glissando, Ross Gorman
cues.text: Ross Gorman’s clarinet rises from a low trill to a high B♭ in one continuous glissando. Gershwin had written a scale. Gorman turned it into a glissando during rehearsal, and Gershwin kept it.
cues.evidence: Jim Farrington, National Recording Registry essay, p. 2, identifies Gorman, the low trill, the rise to concert B-flat and the rehearsal origin of the glissando. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Aeolian Hall, 1924
cues.text: On 12 February 1924 Gershwin played the piano in New York’s Aeolian Hall while Whiteman’s band gave the première of his new Rhapsody. The concert was called “An Experiment in Modern Music”. They made this record four months later, on 10 June 1924.
cues.evidence: The Gershwin estate gives the première’s date, venue and performers; Farrington’s National Recording Registry essay, pp. 1–2, names the concert and dates the recording to 10 June 1924. https://gershwin.com/publications/rhapsody-in-blue/ https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: Scherzo, “Train” and “Stride” themes
cues.text: The faster section combines repeated train-like rhythms with stride piano, in which the left hand jumps between bass notes and chords. To fit the music onto two sides, the record omits the ‘Shuffle’ tune and the third cadenza. After the piano’s stride solo it moves almost directly to the slow melody.
cues.evidence: David Schiff, Gershwin: Rhapsody in Blue (Cambridge University Press), pp. 7–9, Table 1: the scherzo begins with the “Train” theme at rehearsal 9, followed by “Stride” at rehearsal 12; column G marks the 1924 recording’s cuts, from the “Shuffle” at rehearsal 14 and from bar 196 to bar 298, which takes in Cadenza 3 and most of the grand cadenza before the slow movement at rehearsal 28. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Grofé’s orchestration for Whiteman’s band
cues.text: Ferde Grofé turned Gershwin’s two-piano draft into parts for Whiteman’s players, taking pages as Gershwin finished them. He knew their instruments and their individual strengths. The clarinet and trumpet solos were written for a band whose players also made dance records.
cues.evidence: Farrington’s National Recording Registry essay, pp. 1–2, describes the page-by-page orchestration, Grofé’s familiarity with Whiteman’s players and the distinctive playing of Ross Gorman and trumpeter Henry Busse. https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

cues.title: Slow section, melody in E major
cues.text: The slow section opens with a long melody in E major, which the band sustains across whole phrases. The piano later takes the melody over before the closing return of earlier themes.
cues.evidence: Schiff, Gershwin: Rhapsody in Blue, pp. 8–9, Table 1, places the slow section at rehearsal 28 and its piano version later in the same section; p. 9 identifies the melody as the E-major “Love” tune. https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/59539/excerpt/9780521559539_excerpt.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Victor advertisement, Chicago Tribune, 1924
cues.text: Victor advertised the two-sided Rhapsody for $1.50 in the Chicago Tribune on 5 September 1924. The record lasts about nine minutes. Roughly a third of the score was cut to fit the two sides.
cues.evidence: Victor’s advertisement, Chicago Tribune, 5 September 1924, p. 17, lists both parts as Victor 55225 at $1.50; Farrington, p. 2, documents the cuts. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Victor_Records_ad,_Sept_5,_1924_in_Chicago_Tribune.jpg https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/RhapsodyInBlue.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: George Gershwin (piano), Paul Whiteman Concert Orchestra (jazz band), Paul Whiteman (conductor)
fields.note: The Library of Congress credits Gershwin as pianist and Whiteman as leader. Farrington’s essay additionally identifies Ross Gorman’s clarinet and Henry Busse’s trumpet. No complete session personnel list is asserted.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Gershwin’s 1924 acoustic recording with Paul Whiteman’s band, in Ferde Grofé’s original jazz-band orchestration; abridged for two sides of Victor 55225
fields.note: The selected source supplies a single, already-joined MP3 of both parts. Contrapunctus has not joined separate 78 sides. It is the complete issued abridgement, not an uncut performance of the score. Schiff’s Table 1 distinguishes these recording cuts from the cuts in the solo-piano arrangement. The three listening sections group the introduction, the faster dances, and the broad melody with its piano continuation and finale; their starts are passage-level editorial estimates, without bar alignment or aural review. The source does not identify the score or parts used at the session.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Recording date of both Victor sides; separate from the September release and the modern upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: City is documented. A particular Victor studio address or room has not been established.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original commercial issue. The image accompanying the selected transfer shows the blue Victor label, but its relationship to the physical copy digitised is unknown.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Two sides of one 12-inch disc. Bolig dates publication to 5 September 1924; the same day’s Chicago Tribune advertisement lists both parts under 55225, price $1.50, beneath the heading ‘Out today’.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Part 1: C-30174, take 1; Part 2: C-30173, take 2
fields.note: The side-specific Library of Congress catalogue records and Bolig’s discography agree on these matrix/take assignments, which are preferred here. Farrington’s essay reverses the issued take numbers in its final paragraph. The selected upload supplies no runout photographs or transfer log, so its particular pressing and stampers remain unidentified.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Internet Archive identifies an uploader but gives no disc-transfer or restoration credit. The uploaded filename resembles a video title; that alone does not establish a transfer engineer or source chain before this upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was added on 18 March 2024. This is an upload date, not an established digitisation or restoration date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The archive lists the single MP3 as an original upload, with format ‘VBR MP3’. Playback equipment, stylus, speed, equalisation, noise reduction, pitch correction, and the method used to join the two sides are undocumented. No additional audio editing was performed for the Hall.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the United States: Gershwin’s 1924 composition and Grofé’s original 1924 jazz-band setting
fields.note: IMSLP identifies first publication of the two-piano score in 1924 and explicitly distinguishes the US-public-domain 1924 jazz-band setting from the later 1942 symphonic orchestration. This assessment is confined to the original version heard here. Grofé’s orchestrations remain protected in many other countries; no worldwide clearance or permission for modern editions is asserted.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial United States public domain from 1 January 2025, on the documented published-1924 basis
fields.note: Victor 55225 was commercially published on 5 September 1924. Under 17 USC 1401(a)(2)(A) and (B)(ii), the 95-year period plus five-year transition ended on 31 December 2024. The archive supplies no Creative Commons licence. This is a statutory US term assessment of the historical recording, not a worldwide licence; no independent creative restoration claim is documented in the upload.

composer.epithet: Composer who brought Broadway rhythms into the concerto, known for the clarinet slide that became the calling card of American concert music.

composer.background:
In May 1914 a fifteen-year-old pianist went to work for Jerome H. Remick and Company in New York, playing songs to sell them. George Gershwin earned fifteen dollars a week. He could sight-read, transpose and keep a tune attractive through another repetition. Four years earlier his family had bought a piano for his elder brother Ira, and George surprised them by sitting down and playing it; he had been experimenting on the piano at a friend’s house. He was born in Brooklyn on 26 September 1898 to Russian-Jewish immigrants. His first professional work was at a publisher’s keyboard, where a song had to sell to a customer standing beside the piano.

Charles Hambitzer was his piano teacher. Gershwin later called him “the first great musical influence in my life”. He attended concerts by pianists including Leopold Godowsky and Josef Lhévinne, and studied theory with Edward Kilenyi. After leaving school he went on studying, and in the summer of 1921 he took courses in Romantic music and elementary orchestration at Columbia University.
